posts.quote: OUR LEMONADE STAND SOLD TEN CUPS A DAY, AND NINE OF THEM WENT TO MOM AND THE NEIGHBORS.
posts.caption: We built it out of a card table and a cardboard sign with the L written backward. The lemonade was mostly sugar and optimism, and the ice melted before the first customer ever showed up. Mom bought the first cup and acted like it was the best thing she had ever tasted. The neighbors came next, one by one, and every one of them said it needed a little more sugar and paid a full dime anyway. By supper we had a coffee can of nickels and a sunburn, and we thought we were in business for life.
posts.first: My brother and I ran a stand for one whole summer and made a dollar and sixty cents. We split it down the middle and I think we were prouder of that than of anything we did for years after. Mrs. Haskell next door bought a cup every single day and never once told us how bad it was.

posts.quote: THE BREAD BOX SAT ON THE COUNTER, AND EVERYBODY KNEW THE LAST SLICE WAS SPOKEN FOR.
posts.caption: The bread box had a rolltop lid that rattled every time somebody went in for a slice. It held one store loaf at a time, plus a heel nobody wanted and a few sweet rolls Mom was saving for company. You learned early that the last slice was never really the last slice. It was already promised to Dad's lunch, and he would check for it before he took his coat off. If you took it anyway, you ate it standing very still, hoping nobody had counted.
posts.first: My mother kept a loaf of Wonder Bread in ours and a sleeve of saltines she insisted weren't there. I once ate the last slice and she knew before I got the lid down. She never said a word, she just made Dad's sandwich out of the heel and let me think about it.

posts.quote: THE SLED HUNG IN THE GARAGE ALL YEAR, AND THE FIRST SNOW MADE IT THE MOST VALUABLE THING WE OWNED.
posts.caption: It had wooden slats and red steel runners, and it spent eleven months hanging on a nail between the rakes. The first real snowfall, it came down off that nail like a king returning from exile. Dad waxed the runners with a candle stub while we pulled on three pairs of socks. Every hill in town was fair game, and the steepest one had a fence at the bottom that we simply chose not to think about. You came home with frozen mittens, a red nose, and a very specific kind of tired.
posts.first: Ours was a Flexible Flyer my dad bought secondhand and painted himself. My sister steered and I held on for dear life. We went down Miller's Hill so many times that winter I think we wore a groove in it.

posts.character: Old jobs and skills (the corner store)
posts.quote: THE CORNER STORE / WHERE THE OWNER KNEW YOUR NAME AND YOUR MOTHER'S ORDER
posts.caption: The bell over the door jingled before you got both feet inside. Mr. Callahan was already reaching for the bread because he knew exactly what Mom wanted. He kept a running tab in a little green book, and the neighbors paid up on Fridays. The penny candy sat in glass jars at kid height, and he pretended not to watch while you made your choice. He knew who was sick, who was out of work, and whose son was coming home from the service. A grocery store today could never know that much about you.
posts.first: We had a store like that on the corner of Elm and Third. My mother sent me down with a list and a dollar, and Mr. Callahan always sent me home with something extra in the bag. I never found out who paid for it.

posts.quote: MONDAY MEANT THE WRINGER WASHER, AND MOM WATCHED THAT WRINGER LIKE A HAWK.
posts.caption: The wringer washer lived on the back porch and came out every Monday morning like clockwork. It shook the whole floor and sloshed soapy water over the rim, and the wringer on top took no prisoners. Mom fed the clothes through one at a time with a wooden stick and a lot of respect. We were told once, firmly, to keep our hands far away, and nobody needed to be told twice. By noon the sheets were on the line and the porch smelled like soap and bleach.
posts.first: My aunt caught her sleeve in one once and never fully trusted a machine again. Mom had a story for every one of those washers, and none of them ended well for the shirts. I still think of Mondays as laundry days.
